transcription.tex: This chapter applies first- and second-order differential equations in practical settings.
1. First-order modelling\par A particle has acceleration \(a=t+3v/t\), \(t>0\), and \(v=0\) when \(t=2\). Show \(v=ct^3-t^2\), finding \(c\).
2. Simple harmonic motion\par Acceleration towards a central point is proportional to displacement:\[\ddot x=-\omega^2x.\]
3. Damped and forced harmonic motion\par Model damping forces and additional external forces.
4. Coupled first-order equations\par Differential-equation versions of simultaneous equations, including population models:\[\dot x=ax+by,\quad\dot y=cx+dy.\]

transcription.tex: Pure Year 2 introduced forming and solving first-order models. Here these may have the form \(y^{\prime}+Py=Q\). Motion gives examples such as \(a=dv/dt\).

A particle starts from rest at \(O\), moving along a line with acceleration \(6/(t+2)^2\) m s\(^{-2}\), \(t\ge0\).\par (a) Find its velocity.\par (b) Show its displacement at \(t=6\) is \(18-12\ln2\) m.
\[\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac6{(t+2)^2}\Rightarrow v=-\frac6{t+2}+c.\]\[v(0)=0\Rightarrow c=3\Rightarrow v=3-\frac6{t+2}.\]
A particle has acceleration \(a=t+3v/t\), \(t>0\). Given \(v(2)=0\), show \(v=ct^3-t^2\), finding \(c\).\par Hint: write in the form \(dv/dt+Pv=Q\) and multiply by \(e^{\int P\,dt}\).
\[\frac{dv}{dt}-\frac3tv=t\]\[\mathrm{IF}=e^{\int-3/t\,dt}=e^{-3\ln t}=t^{-3}\]\[\frac d{dt}(t^{-3}v)=t^{-2}\]\[t^{-3}v=-t^{-1}+c.\]\[v(2)=0\Rightarrow c=\tfrac12\]\[v=\tfrac12t^3-t^2.\]

transcription.tex: A tank initially contains 1000 litres of pure water. Liquid leaves at 30 litres/hour and solution enters at 40 litres/hour, containing 4 grams of copper sulphate per litre. It mixes immediately throughout the tank. Let \(x\) be the copper sulphate mass in grams after \(t\) hours.\par (a) Show \(dx/dt=160-3x/(100+t)\).\par (b) Find the mass after 6 hours.\par (c) Explain how the model could be refined.

Volume: \(1000+40t-30t=1000+10t\) litres.\par Concentration: \(x/(1000+10t)\) g/litre.\par Inflow: \(40\times4=160\) g/hour.\par Outflow: \(30x/(1000+10t)=3x/(100+t)\) g/hour.\[\frac{dx}{dt}=160-\frac{3x}{100+t}.\]
Allow for the time taken for the copper sulphate to disperse, instead of assuming instantaneous mixing.

transcription.tex: \(O\) is the centre of oscillation. Moving away from \(O\), the particle slows down because its acceleration is towards \(O\). Doubling displacement doubles acceleration magnitude. It is not constant as in uniform gravity.

Simple harmonic motion (SHM) has acceleration towards a fixed point on the line of motion, proportional to displacement from that point:\[\ddot x=-\omega^2x.\]Dots mean time derivatives; \(\ddot x\) is acceleration. The minus sign makes it restoring. \(\omega>0\) is angular frequency in radians/second, and \(\omega^2\) the proportionality constant.\par The chain rule gives\[\ddot x=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}=v\frac{dv}{dx}.\]This helps solve the motion equation.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: A particle has SHM about \(O\), with maximum displacement \(a\).\par (a) Show \(v^2=\omega^2(a^2-x^2)\).

\[\ddot x=-\omega^2x\Rightarrow v\frac{dv}{dx}=-\omega^2x\]\[\int v\,dv=-\int\omega^2x\,dx\]\[\tfrac12v^2=-\tfrac12\omega^2x^2+c.\]At maximum displacement \(x=a\), \(v=0\), so \(c=\tfrac12\omega^2a^2\).\[\tfrac12v^2=-\tfrac12\omega^2x^2+\tfrac12\omega^2a^2\]\[v^2=\omega^2(a^2-x^2).\]
Complex numbers provide a practical tool for solving this applied motion equation.
(b) Show \(x=a\sin(\omega t+\alpha)\), with arbitrary phase \(\alpha\).

\[\ddot x+\omega^2x=0,\quad m^2+\omega^2=0\]\[m=\pm i\omega\Rightarrow x=A\cos\omega t+B\sin\omega t\]\[=R\sin(\omega t+\alpha).\]Using Pure Year 2 trigonometry, \(R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\). Since the amplitude is \(a\),\[x=a\sin(\omega t+\alpha).\]

Displacement follows a sine wave. Amplitude is maximum displacement. The phase \(\alpha\) controls translation; \(\alpha=0\) starts at equilibrium. Period \(T=2\pi/\omega\); \(\omega=1\) gives one oscillation per \(2\pi\) seconds.

transcription.tex: A particle moves along a line with \(\ddot x=-4x\). At \(t=0\), \(x=1\) m and \(v=4\) m s\(^{-1}\).\par (a) Find displacement after \(t\) seconds.\par (b) Find maximum displacement from \(O\).\par Hint: find constants in the sine/cosine form before combining.
\[\ddot x+4x=0\Rightarrow m^2+4=0\Rightarrow m=\pm2i\]\[x=A\cos2t+B\sin2t.\]\[x(0)=1\Rightarrow A=1\]\[v=-2\sin2t+2B\cos2t\]\[v(0)=4\Rightarrow B=2\]\[x=\cos2t+2\sin2t.\]
\[x=\sqrt5\sin(2t+0.4636\ldots).\]Maximum displacement is \(\sqrt5\) m.

A particle joins two identical elastic springs fixed at \(A,B\). It is held at a point \(C\) between them, with \(AC\ne BC\), and released from rest. Let \(x\) be displacement from equilibrium \(O\), with release point \(C\) at \(x=0.4\) m. The model is \(\ddot x=-25x\).\par (a) Describe the motion.\par (b) Given \(x(0)=0.4,v(0)=0\), solve for \(x(t)\).\par (c) State the period and maximum speed.
Simple harmonic motion.
\[m^2+25=0\Rightarrow m=\pm5i\]\[x=A\cos5t+B\sin5t,\quad A=0.4\]\[v=-2\sin5t+5B\cos5t,\quad B=0\]\[x=0.4\cos5t.\]
\[T=\frac{2\pi}5\text{ s},\quad v=-2\sin5t.\]Maximum speed is \(2\) m s\(^{-1}\).

transcription.tex: In practice the amplitude often decreases over time, so there is another force: damping, opposing velocity and proportional to its magnitude.\par The spring’s elastic force is called the restoring force.

Without damping, spring extension/compression gives a restoring acceleration proportional to displacement, resulting in sinusoidal motion.\par With damping:\[\ddot x=-k\dot x-\omega^2x\]\[\ddot x+k\dot x+\omega^2x=0,\quad k>0.\]The roots of the auxiliary equation determine the type of damped motion.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: \[\ddot x+k\dot x+\omega^2x=0,\quad k,\omega>0.\]\[m^2+km+\omega^2=0.\]The discriminant determines the nature of the roots.
Distinct real roots:\[k^2-4\omega^2>0\]
\[x=Ae^{-\alpha t}+Be^{-\beta t},\quad\alpha,\beta>0.\]
Heavy damping: no repeated oscillations.
Equal real roots:\[k^2-4\omega^2=0\]
Critical damping: the boundary between oscillatory and non-oscillatory motion.
Complex conjugate roots:\[k^2-4\omega^2<0\]
\[x=e^{-kt/2}(A\cos\Omega t+B\sin\Omega t)\]\[\Omega=\sqrt{\omega^2-k^2/4}.\]
Light damping: oscillations with decreasing amplitude.

transcription.tex: A particle of mass 0.5 kg moves horizontally. Its displacement from \(O\) is \(x\) m and velocity \(v\) m s\(^{-1}\). A restoring force has signed value \(-8x\) N and resistance \(-4v\) N. Initially \(x=1.5\) and it moves in increasing \(x\) with speed 4 m s\(^{-1}\).\par (a) Show \(\ddot x+8\dot x+16x=0\).\par (b) Find \(x(1)\).

\[m^2+8m+16=0\Rightarrow m=-4\]\[x=(A+Bt)e^{-4t}.\]\[x(0)=1.5\Rightarrow A=1.5\]\[v=Be^{-4t}-4(A+Bt)e^{-4t}\]\[v(0)=4\Rightarrow B=10\]\[x=(1.5+10t)e^{-4t}\]\[x(1)=11.5e^{-4}\approx0.211\text{ m (3 s.f.)}.\]Equal roots give critical damping.

transcription.tex: A particle hangs in equilibrium on a light elastic string fixed at \(A\). It is pulled down into a resisting liquid and released from rest. While the string is taut and the particle remains submerged,\[\ddot x+6k\dot x+5k^2x=0,\quad k>0.\]Find the general solution and type of damping.
\[m^2+6km+5k^2=(m+5k)(m+k)=0\]\[m=-5k,-k\]\[x=Ae^{-5kt}+Be^{-kt}.\]Two distinct real roots give heavy damping.

A particle hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic spring fixed at \(A\). It is pulled down and released from rest, with resistance proportional to speed. Its displacement from equilibrium obeys\[\ddot x+2k\dot x+2k^2x=0,\quad k>0.\]Find the general solution and period of oscillation.

\[m^2+2km+2k^2=0\]\[m=\frac{-2k\pm\sqrt{4k^2-8k^2}}2=-k\pm ik\]\[x=e^{-kt}(A\cos kt+B\sin kt).\]\[T=\frac{2\pi}k.\]The coefficient of \(t\) in the sine/cosine gives the angular frequency of the oscillation.

transcription.tex: An additional external force produces forced harmonic motion:\[\ddot x+k\dot x+\omega^2x=f(t).\]This is non-homogeneous, so use CF + PI.\par A particle of mass 1.5 kg moves on the \(x\)-axis under restoring force \(-7.5x\) N, resistance \(-6\dot x\) N and external force \(12\sin t\) N in the positive direction. Initially \(x=5,\dot x=2\).\par (a) Show \(\ddot x+4\dot x+5x=8\sin t\).\par (b) Find \(x(t)\).\par (c) Describe the motion for large \(t\).
\[-7.5x-6\dot x+12\sin t=1.5\ddot x\]\[\ddot x+5x+4\dot x=8\sin t\]\[\ddot x+4\dot x+5x=8\sin t.\]
As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-2t}\to0\). Hence the transient decays and\[x\sim\sin t-\cos t=\sqrt2\sin(t-\pi/4).\]The limiting motion is SHM with amplitude \(\sqrt2\) m and period \(2\pi\) s.

\[m^2+4m+5=0\Rightarrow m=-2\pm i\]\[x_c=e^{-2t}(A\cos t+B\sin t).\]Try \(x_p=p\sin t+q\cos t\):\[\dot x_p=p\cos t-q\sin t,\quad\ddot x_p=-p\sin t-q\cos t.\]\[(-p\sin t-q\cos t)+4(p\cos t-q\sin t)\]\[+5(p\sin t+q\cos t)=8\sin t.\]\[p+q=0,\quad p-q=2\Rightarrow p=1,q=-1.\]\[x=e^{-2t}(A\cos t+B\sin t)+\sin t-\cos t.\]\[x(0)=5\Rightarrow A-1=5\Rightarrow A=6\]\[\dot x(0)=2\Rightarrow-2A+B+1=2\Rightarrow B=13\]\[x=e^{-2t}(6\cos t+13\sin t)+\sin t-\cos t.\]

transcription.tex: A particle \(P\) is attached to end \(A\) of a light elastic string \(AB\), initially at rest on a smooth horizontal plane. At \(t=0\), end \(B\) moves at constant speed \(U\) in direction \(AB\). Air resistance is proportional to the particle’s speed. For the prescribed model, displacement \(x\) from the initial position obeys\[\ddot x+2k\dot x+k^2x=2kU,\quad k>0.\]Find \(x(t)\), using initial rest: \(x(0)=0,\dot x(0)=0\).

\[m^2+2km+k^2=(m+k)^2=0\]\[\mathrm{CF}=(A+Bt)e^{-kt}.\]Since the forcing is constant, try \(x_p=c\):\[\dot x_p=\ddot x_p=0,\quad k^2c=2kU\Rightarrow c=\frac{2U}k.\]\[x=(A+Bt)e^{-kt}+\frac{2U}k.\]\[x(0)=0\Rightarrow A=-\frac{2U}k\]\[\dot x=-k(A+Bt)e^{-kt}+Be^{-kt}\]\[\dot x(0)=0\Rightarrow0=-kA+B\Rightarrow B=-2U\]\[x=\left(-\frac{2U}k-2Ut\right)e^{-kt}+\frac{2U}k.\]

transcription.tex: Coupled population models describe interacting species. Let \(x\) be bears and \(y\) fish. Bear population growth depends on bear numbers, prey availability and possibly seasonal effects such as increased breeding.

Fish growth depends on predator numbers (more bears may mean faster decline), fish numbers and other time-dependent factors.\par We study a linear model. Classical Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations are nonlinear; this linear system is a simplified model.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: \[\dot x=ax+by+f(t),\quad\dot y=cx+dy+g(t).\]Homogeneous if \(f=g=0\) for all \(t\).\par Strategy: 1. Make \(y\) the subject of the first equation and differentiate. 2. Substitute in the second equation and solve the resulting second-order equation for \(x\). 3. Differentiate the result and use the first rearrangement to find \(y\).

A survey of a remote Canadian island began in 2010. After \(t\) years, bear and fish populations \(x,y\) obey\[\dot x=0.3x+0.1y,\quad\dot y=-0.1x+0.5y.\]\par (a) Show \(\ddot x-0.8\dot x+0.16x=0\).\par (b) Find the general solution for bears.\par (c) Find the general solution for fish.\par (d) Initially 5 bears and 20 fish: predict bears in 2020.\par (e) Comment on suitability.
\[y=10\dot x-3x\Rightarrow\dot y=10\ddot x-3\dot x\]\[10\ddot x-3\dot x=-0.1x+0.5(10\dot x-3x)\]\[10\ddot x-8\dot x+1.6x=0\]\[\ddot x-0.8\dot x+0.16x=0.\]
\[x(0)=5\Rightarrow A=5\]\[y(0)=20\Rightarrow5+10B=20\Rightarrow B=1.5\]\[x(10)=(5+15)e^4\approx1092\text{ bears}.\]
Both populations grow without limit, so this is unlikely to remain realistic.

transcription.tex: Two barrels contain contaminated water. At time \(t\) seconds, contaminant amounts in \(A,B\) are \(x,y\) ml. Contaminant enters \(A\) at 5 ml/s; water moves both ways through hoses and also drains from \(A\) out of the system. The model is\[\dot x=5+\tfrac49y-\tfrac17x\qquad(1)\]\[\dot y=\tfrac3{70}x-\tfrac49y\qquad(2).\]Show \(630\ddot y+370\dot y+28y=135\).\par Hint: make \(x\) the subject in (2), differentiate and substitute into (1).

\[\dot y+\tfrac49y=\tfrac3{70}x\]\[x=\tfrac{70}3\dot y+\tfrac{280}{27}y\]\[\dot x=\tfrac{70}3\ddot y+\tfrac{280}{27}\dot y.\]Substitute into (1):\[\tfrac{70}3\ddot y+\tfrac{280}{27}\dot y=5+\tfrac49y-\tfrac17(\tfrac{70}3\dot y+\tfrac{280}{27}y)\]\[70\ddot y+\tfrac{280}9\dot y=15+\tfrac43y-10\dot y-\tfrac{40}9y\]\[630\ddot y+280\dot y=135+12y-90\dot y-40y\]\[630\ddot y+370\dot y+28y=135.\]
